diagnosis_steps: Check that the ice maker is turned on — look for an on/off switch or wire bail arm on the side of the ice maker; the arm should be in the down position.
Confirm the freezer temperature is at or below 0°F (-18°C). Warm freezer temps are the #1 cause of no ice.
Inspect the water supply line behind the refrigerator for kinks or pinches; straighten any you find.
Replace the water filter if it is older than 6 months — a clogged filter restricts water flow to the ice maker.
Test the water inlet valve for continuity with a multimeter; replace it if it reads open (no continuity).
If all the above pass, replace the ice maker assembly itself.
Check that the refrigerator is plugged in and the circuit breaker is not tripped.
Verify the temperature controls are set correctly — fresh food should be around 37°F and freezer at 0°F.
Listen for the condenser fan (at the back or bottom) — if you don't hear it, the fan motor may be faulty.
Inspect the door gaskets for tears or gaps; a poor seal lets warm air in continuously.
Check the evaporator fan in the freezer compartment — if it's not running, the compressor start relay may be faulty.
Test the compressor start relay by shaking it — a rattling noise means it has failed.
If none of the above resolves the issue, the compressor itself may need professional service.
Locate the source of the leak — check if it is from the water dispenser, the ice maker, or from under the refrigerator.
If leaking at the dispenser or ice maker: inspect the water supply line and inlet valve connections for loose fittings.
Check the drain pan under the refrigerator — if cracked or overflowing, it will drip on the floor.
Inspect the defrost drain tube in the freezer — a clogged drain will cause water to pool and leak.
If the water supply line is cracked or has a loose compression fitting, replace or tighten it.
Check the water inlet valve for cracks or a faulty seal.

Identify the type of noise: clicking usually points to the compressor start relay; buzzing to the ice maker or inlet valve; rattling to a loose drain pan or condenser fan; squealing to the evaporator fan motor.
For clicking: shake the compressor start relay — if it rattles, replace it.
For buzzing near the ice maker: the water inlet valve solenoid may be failing; test with a multimeter.
For rattling: check that the drain pan is seated properly and the condenser coils are not vibrating against anything.
For squealing or grinding: the evaporator fan motor bearings may be worn — replace the motor.
Check that the spray arms spin freely — remove them and look for clogged holes; use a toothpick to clear any blockages.
Inspect the spray arm for cracks — a cracked arm loses pressure and cannot clean effectively.
Clean the filter assembly at the bottom of the dishwasher; a clogged filter dramatically reduces cleaning.
Verify water temperature is at least 120°F — run hot water at the sink before starting the cycle.
Check the detergent dispenser opens properly during the wash cycle.
If the motor makes noise but water pressure is weak, the wash pump may be failing.
Identify where the leak originates — from the door, under the unit, or from connections at the back.
If leaking from the door: inspect the door gasket for tears, cracks, or sections that have come loose; replace if damaged.
Ensure the dishwasher is level — an unlevel unit can cause water to pool against the door and leak.
Check the door latch — if the door does not close completely, water will spray out.
If leaking from under the unit: inspect the pump hoses and water inlet connections for looseness.
Overfilling can also cause leaks — ensure the float switch inside the tub moves freely.
Confirm the dishwasher is getting power — check the circuit breaker and ensure the unit is plugged in.
Make sure the door is fully latched — dishwashers won't run unless the door latch engages the door switch.
Try a hard reset: turn off the circuit breaker for 60 seconds, then restore power.
Check for a Control Lock or Child Lock indicator on the panel — hold the lock button for 3 seconds to disable.
If the door clicks shut but the unit still won't start, the door latch assembly or door switch may be faulty.
If the control panel is unresponsive or shows an error code, the control board may have failed.
Ensure you are using rinse aid — it is essential for effective drying; refill the dispenser if empty.
Check that the heated dry option is selected — some cycles default to air-dry only.
Plastic items naturally retain water more than glass or ceramic; this is normal behavior.
Test the heating element for continuity with a multimeter — if it reads open, the element has failed.
Inspect the high-limit thermostat on the heating element — a blown thermostat will disable the heat.
If the element has continuity but still produces no heat, the control board may not be activating it.
Check that the refrigerator is plugged in and the outlet has power — test with another device.
Check the circuit breaker or fuse for the refrigerator's circuit; reset or replace if tripped.
Listen for a clicking sound from the back — repeated clicking usually means a faulty compressor overload relay.
Remove the overload relay from the compressor and shake it; a rattling sound confirms it has failed — replace it.
Test the temperature control thermostat by turning it from the lowest to highest setting; if you don't hear a click, the thermostat may be defective.
If the compressor hums but doesn't run, the start capacitor may need replacement.
If none of the above applies, the main control board may have failed.
Confirm the water supply line behind the refrigerator is connected and the shutoff valve is open.
Replace the water filter if it is older than 6 months — a clogged filter is the most common cause.
Check that the dispenser lock is not enabled — hold the lock button for 3 seconds to toggle it.
Press the dispenser paddle firmly; if there is no sound at all, the dispenser switch or actuator may be faulty.
Test the water inlet valve for continuity with a multimeter — replace it if it reads open.
If water pressure from the house supply is below 20 psi, the inlet valve will not open.
Inspect the door gasket all the way around for tears, stiffness, or sections that have pulled away from the door — replace if damaged.
Close the door on a piece of paper; if you can pull it out easily, the gasket is not sealing.
Check the door hinges — a sagging door prevents the gasket from seating evenly; adjust or replace the hinge.
Ensure the refrigerator is level front-to-back so doors close under their own weight.
If the gasket is intact and the door seals well, the mullion or anti-sweat heater between the doors may be faulty.
Open the door and press the door switch manually — if the light turns on, the switch itself is stuck or broken.
Check that the light bulb is not burned out; replace it with the correct wattage specified in the owner's manual.
Test the door switch for continuity with a multimeter — replace it if it reads open when pressed.
If the light uses an LED module rather than a bulb, the module itself may need replacement.
If none of the above resolves the issue, the main control board may not be supplying power to the light circuit.
Check the temperature setting — the fresh food section should be around 37°F; adjust the thermostat if it is set too low.
Test the temperature control thermostat by turning it to the warmest setting; if the compressor doesn't stop running, the thermostat may be stuck.
Inspect the thermistor (temperature sensor) — use a multimeter to check its resistance matches the chart in the service manual; replace if out of range.
Check the damper or air inlet door that controls airflow from the freezer — if stuck open, too much cold air enters the fresh food section.
If the compressor runs continuously without cycling off, the main control board may be at fault.
Check the door gaskets for a tight seal — a leaking gasket lets warm air in constantly, forcing the compressor to run non-stop.
Make sure the condenser coils (at the back or bottom) are clean — dust buildup makes the compressor work harder and longer.
Check that the condenser fan is running; a failed fan motor causes the refrigerator to run continuously.
Inspect the defrost system — if frost builds up on the evaporator, the refrigerator will struggle to cool and run too long. Check the defrost heater and defrost thermostat.
Verify the refrigerator is not overfilled and has adequate airflow around the contents.
Adjust the freezer temperature control — 0°F is the recommended setting; turn it toward a warmer setting.
Test the temperature control thermostat — if the compressor runs continuously and does not cycle off, the thermostat may be stuck in the closed position.
Check the thermistor resistance with a multimeter; replace it if the reading is out of spec for the current temperature.
Inspect the damper between the freezer and fresh food sections — if stuck closed it concentrates all cold air in the freezer.
If all above check out, the main control board may be sending incorrect signals to the compressor.
Identify the type of noise: grinding usually means debris in the pump; thumping or banging often means the spray arm is hitting dishes or a utensil fell through the rack.
Remove the lower rack and spin the spray arm — if it is blocked or cracked, replace it.
Check for hard items (broken glass, seeds, bone fragments) in the filter and pump area at the bottom; remove any debris.
If you hear a loud grinding or humming from below, the wash pump motor bearings may be worn — replace the pump and motor assembly.
A squealing noise during draining points to a worn drain pump impeller — replace the drain pump.
Rattling from the door area may mean a loose door spring or hinge — inspect and tighten or replace.
Try closing the door firmly — if it does not latch, inspect the door latch assembly for broken plastic tabs or a worn strike.
Test the door switch with a multimeter for continuity when the door is closed — no continuity means the switch is faulty.
Check the door hinges and springs — a sagging door will not align with the latch; adjust or replace the springs.
Inspect the door gasket; a thick buildup of detergent or food residue can prevent the door from closing flush.
If the door latches but the dishwasher still won't run, the door switch or wiring to the control board may be the issue.
Check the drain hose for kinks or clogs — straighten the hose and clear any blockage.
Ensure the drain hose is installed with a high loop or connects to an air gap to prevent backflow.
Clean the dishwasher filter at the bottom of the tub — a clogged filter is a very common cause of standing water.
Check the knockout plug in the garbage disposal inlet — if the dishwasher was recently connected to a new disposal, the plug may not have been removed.
Test the drain pump by starting a drain cycle and listening — if silent, the pump motor may be burned out; replace the drain pump.
If the pump runs but water does not move, the pump impeller may be broken or jammed with debris.

symptom: dishwasher will not fill with water
diagnosis_steps: Confirm the water supply valve under the sink is fully open.
Check the water inlet valve screen for debris — sediment can clog the screen and restrict flow; clean or replace the valve.
Test the water inlet valve solenoid for continuity with a multimeter — replace it if it reads open.
Inspect the float switch at the bottom of the tub — if the float is stuck in the raised position, it signals 'full' and prevents filling; free the float or replace the switch.
Check the door switch — the dishwasher will not fill unless the door is latched and the switch is closed.
If the control panel shows an error code, look it up in the service manual; some codes indicate a fill timeout.
Make sure you are using dishwasher-specific detergent and not overfilling the dispenser — overfilling prevents the door from opening.
Check that the dispenser door is not blocked by a large item in the lower rack.
Inspect the dispenser door spring and latch — if the spring is broken, the door will not pop open during the wash cycle.
Test the wax motor (bi-metal actuator) that triggers the dispenser door — if it does not activate, replace it.
If the dispenser door opens but detergent remains, water may not be reaching the dispenser area — check the spray arms for clogs.
A faulty timer or control board may not be sending the signal to open the dispenser at the right point in the cycle.
